summary: A 1969 description of how to implement the host-to-host procedures in GORDO, a host system. It covers connections and links, message structure and user transactions, and then how to realise them in that system. It was replaced by RFC 33.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 11 describes how the GORDO operating system at UCLA organized host-to-host network communication. A Network program managed user connections and messages, while a Handler exchanged message words with the IMP hardware; RFC 33 later obsoleted this memo.

questions: how did gordo manage host-to-host connections
what was the difference between primary and auxiliary connections
what did the gordo network handler do
subtitle: How the GORDO operating system implemented host-to-host network procedures.

tldr.problem: Multiple users on one host needed to share network facilities while communicating with users on remote hosts.
tldr.mechanism: GORDO uses a Network program to manage connections and messages and a Handler interrupt routine to exchange messages with the IMP hardware.
tldr.outcome: RFC 11 was obsoleted by RFC 33 and records a GORDO implementation of host-to-host procedures.

sections.title: Connections, Links, and Message Types
sections.content:
A logical connection links users at remote hosts and appears full-duplex to them. Each connection uses a pair of directional links, one to transmit and one to receive. Users work with connections; the Network programs manage the links.

The RFC distinguishes control, primary, and auxiliary connections. A control connection carries messages between Network programs. A primary connection is established first between a pair of users. Auxiliary connections can be opened alongside it for larger volumes of data.
sections.plainLanguage: Users see a two-way connection, while the operating system manages separate links for sending and receiving. Control connections coordinate setup; primary and auxiliary connections carry user communication.

sections.title: Messages and User Transactions
sections.content:
A message can be up to 8095 bits. The described format has a 32-bit leader with message type, source and destination host, and link number; a marker; message text; a 16-bit checksum; and padding where needed. The checksum covers the message except the leader and padding.

The user transactions include opening a primary connection, opening auxiliary connections, transmitting over a connection, and closing connections. Network programs exchange control messages such as ENQ, ACK, and EOT to establish or delete connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages have a leader that identifies their route and link, followed by the text and a checksum. Users request connections and transfers; the Network programs exchange control messages to carry out those requests.

sections.title: The GORDO Network and Handler Programs
sections.content:
The Handler is a core-resident I/O interrupt routine that reads messages from and writes messages to the IMP-HOST hardware interface. The Network program is a regular GORDO process that opens and closes connections, handles incoming control messages, formats outgoing messages, and delivers incoming messages to users.

The programs share buffer pages. The RFC describes allocation tables for tracking free outgoing links, connection state, and incoming links. A user process places data in a shared output buffer and wakes the Network process; the Network formats the message and passes it to the Handler.
sections.plainLanguage: The Handler moves message words between the host and the IMP. The Network program handles user requests, prepares messages, and sends incoming messages to the right user.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 11 describes host-to-host procedures and their implementation in GORDO. The unit metadata identifies RFC 33 as the document that obsoleted it.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo documents one implementation of early host-to-host networking. RFC 33 later obsoleted it.
